findings.truth: Greek temple entrances were usually east-facing, but there were exceptions; the direction is not universal.

findings.claim: The altar stood outside the temple entirely, always to the east.
findings.truth: The altar was outside the temple; it was not always to the east.

findings.truth: An altar’s eastward position was not universal, so it cannot be a required feature of an answer.

findings.claim: A fulfilled promise to dedicate an offering was called a vow in Latin
findings.truth: The Latin term is votum; it means a vow or promise and can also denote what fulfils it.
findings.evidence: Votum (fetched): defines votum and its meanings in Roman religion.

findings.claim: This principle of piacula (atonement) meant that religious officials were extremely careful
findings.truth: Piaculum is singular and means an expiatory sacrifice or victim; it is not the name of a principle of ritual correctness.
findings.evidence: Glossary of ancient Roman religion (fetched), piaculum entry; it defines a piaculum as an expiatory sacrifice.

findings.claim: any error required the whole ceremony to be repeated from the beginning
findings.truth: A ritual error could require an expiatory sacrifice; a universal restart rule is too absolute.
findings.evidence: Glossary of ancient Roman religion (fetched): a hostia succidanea followed a failed sacrifice; piaculum was expiatory.

findings.claim: Roman demand for ritual perfection and repetition if error
findings.truth: Roman ritual stressed correct performance, but an error could be addressed with an expiatory sacrifice rather than a universal restart rule.
findings.evidence: Glossary of ancient Roman religion (fetched), piaculum and hostia succidanea entries.

findings.claim: Roman ritual had to be repeated from the beginning if an error was made
findings.truth: An error could require an expiatory sacrifice; the consequence was not invariably a full repetition.
findings.evidence: Glossary of ancient Roman religion (fetched), piaculum and hostia succidanea entries.

findings.claim: Romans required absolute ritual correctness; any mistake invalidated the ceremony.
findings.truth: Roman ritual stressed correct performance, and an error could require an expiatory sacrifice.
findings.evidence: Glossary of ancient Roman religion (fetched), piaculum and hostia succidanea entries.

findings.truth: Cremation was common from the later Republic into the early Empire; inhumation later became more common, and the causes remain uncertain.
